newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian unemployment dips but doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: Austrian unemployment dips but doubts remain.

text.p: Austrian unemployment dipped slightly in June but the outlook mid-to-long-term is far from rosy, despite an EU Amsterdam summit pact tying jobs and economic growth to budget stability, according to economists and unions.

The number of people out of work slipped to 193,796 in June from 210,993 in May, the Social Affairs Ministry said on Tuesday. The percentage jobless figure is due on Wednesday. Last month it stood at 4.4 percent.
"Unemployment is going to stay high," said Gudrun Biffl, labour expert at the semi-official WIFO economic institute.
She said Austria was relatively unprepared for competition from other EU states and that restrictive institutional practices threatened to cost local firms domestic market share.
"I don't think we've got our back to the wall yet but success on the employment front depends on labour organisations' ability to adjust rapidly," she said.

Although unemployment in Austria is relatively low compared with the rest of Europe, the sensitive issue was catapulted to the fore in January when joblessness spiked to a post World War Two high of over 300,000 in a population of eight million.
Since then the figure has declined but fears remain that it will start to grow again with the approach of European economic and monetary union. Austria joined the EU in January 1995.
Civil servants have already staged strikes in protest at pay and job cuts as a result of the government's austerity policies aimed at meeting the Maastricht criteria.
"One hopes with the introduction of the euro and Maastricht coming into effect it will mean the end of fiscal consolidation and consequently an economic upswing," WIFO's Biffl said.
But Austria needed economic growth of at least 2.5 percent to make significant inroads in creating jobs, she added.

WIFO predicts that the country's gross domestic product will rise 1.4 percent in 1997 and 2.2 percent in 1998. Economic growth is expected to be mainly export-led with domestic demand subdued amid falling real incomes.

Ernst Tuechler, economic consultant at the Austrian trade union congress (OeGB), said employees in the services industry, particularly in the overcrowded banking sector, were worried about the potentially negative impact of the introduction of a single currency.
"Our position on monetary union is yes...but," he said. "There will be problems and how are we going to solve them?"
"We feel that the opening up of the markets must also take into account the needs of the job market -- can we employ people, can we integrate them, and house them?" he asked.
Christian Festa, head of statistics at the Chamber of Economy said he believed the problem of unemployment was a structural one.

"Our official interpretation is that the euro will have a positive effect on employment, but to be honest it won't be very strong. I think the cyclical factors are much stronger than the introduction of the euro," he noted.
Festa voiced concern over growing unemployment among the population over 55 years old.
"There is a growing trend towards sending people into early retirement to make way for younger workers and I fear it can only get worse," he said.
